questions.stem:
The curve $C$ has equation
$2x - 4y^2 + 3x^2y = 4x^2 + 8$
The point $P(3, 2)$ lies on $C$.
Find the equation of the normal to $C$ at the point $P$, writing your answer in the form $ax + by + c = 0$ where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are integers to be found.
(7)

parts.text:
The curve $C$ has equation
$2x - 4y^2 + 3x^2y = 4x^2 + 8$
The point $P(3, 2)$ lies on $C$.
Find the equation of the normal to $C$ at the point $P$, writing your answer in the form $ax + by + c = 0$ where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are integers to be found.
(7)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Attempts at chain rule $y^2 \to ...y\frac{dy}{dx}$ where ... is a constant
M1: Attempt at product rule $3x^2y \to ...x^2\frac{dy}{dx}+...xy$ where ... are constants
A1: Correct differentiation $2x-4y^2+3x^2y=4x^2+8 \to 2-8y\frac{dy}{dx}+6xy+3x^2\frac{dy}{dx}=8x$ o.e. You may see $2x-4y^2+3x^2y=4x^2+8 \to 2\,dx-8y\,dy+6xy\,dx+3x^2\,dy=8x\,dx$ o.e. which is fine. Note that $\frac{dy}{dx}=2-8y\frac{dy}{dx}+6xy+3x^2\frac{dy}{dx}-8x$ is A0 unless recovered
M1: Substitutes $x=3, y=2$ into a suitable equation and finds a value for $\frac{dy}{dx}$. It is dependent upon having exactly two $\frac{dy}{dx}$ terms, one from differentiating each of $y^2$ and $x^2y$
A1: $\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{14}{11}$ o.e.
dM1: Dependent upon the previous M. It is for a correct method of finding the equation of the normal at $(3,2)$. Look for $y-2=\text{"}\frac{11}{14}\text{"}(x-3)$ with the negative reciprocal of their $-\frac{14}{11}$ being used. If the form $y=mx+c$ is used they must proceed as far as $c=...$
A1: $11x-14y-5=0$ but accept any integer multiple of this. The "=0" must be seen

questions.stem:
Find the particular solution of the differential equation
$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{4y^2}{\sqrt{4x+5}}$    $x > -\dfrac{5}{4}$
for which  $y = \dfrac{1}{3}$  at  $x = -\dfrac{1}{4}$  giving your answer in the form  $y = \mathrm{f}(x)$
(6)

parts.text:
Find the particular solution of the differential equation
$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{4y^2}{\sqrt{4x+5}}$    $x > -\dfrac{5}{4}$
for which  $y = \dfrac{1}{3}$  at  $x = -\dfrac{1}{4}$  giving your answer in the form  $y = \mathrm{f}(x)$
(6)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: Separates the variables. Note that the "4" may be on either side but must be in the correct place. The $dy$ and $dx$ must be present and in the correct place. Condone missing integral signs
M1: Integrates one side to a correct form. No requirement for $+c$. Look for $\int \frac{1}{y^2}\,dy \to \frac{a}{y}$ or $\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{4x+5}}\,dx \to k\sqrt{4x+5}$ or equivalent
A1: Correct integration for both sides. Allow unsimplified but there is no requirement for $+c$. Look for $-\frac{1}{y}=2\sqrt{4x+5}$ or equivalent such as $-\frac{1}{4y}=\frac{\sqrt{4x+5}}{4\times\frac{1}{2}}$
dM1: Substitutes $y=\frac{1}{3}, x=-\frac{1}{4}$ into their integrated form to find a value for $c$. It is dependent upon having integrated one side to a correct form. Condone this being done following poor re-arrangement
ddM1: Rearranges $\frac{a}{y}=b\sqrt{4x+5}+c$ to $y=....$ using a correct method. Do not allow each term to be inverted. It is dependent upon: integrating BOTH sides to a correct form; substituting $y=\frac{1}{3}, x=-\frac{1}{4}$ into the correct integrated form to find a value for $c$; rearranging $\frac{a}{y}=b\sqrt{4x+5}+c$ to $y=....$ using a correct method but condone sign slips
A1: $y=\dfrac{1}{7-2\sqrt{4x+5}}$ or exact equivalent. E.g. $y=\dfrac{-1}{2(4x+5)^{0.5}-7}$. Do not isw. So if the candidate then writes $y=\frac{1}{7}-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4x+5}}$ it is A0
Official notes (completeness pass):
- $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{4y^2}{\sqrt{4x+5}} \Rightarrow \int \frac{1}{y^2}\,dy=\int \frac{4}{\sqrt{4x+5}}\,dx$ B1
- $-\frac{1}{y}=2\sqrt{4x+5}\,(+c)$ M1, A1; Substitutes $y=\frac{1}{3}, x=-\frac{1}{4} \Rightarrow -3=4+c \Rightarrow c=...$ dM1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the values of the constants $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Attempts a correct identity $3x^3+8x^2-3x-6 \equiv (Ax+B)x(x+3)+C(x+3)+Dx$ o.e. Establishes a method of starting the problem either by attempting a correct identity or attempting to divide the cubic by $x^2+3x$ to obtain a linear quotient. Condone slips in the cubic expression but the intention must be correct
dM1: Correct method for two constants e.g. $x=0, x=-3 \Rightarrow C=..., D=...$. Attempts a correct method to find two constants. An attempt must be made at a correct equation. For the main method this could be via substituting both $x=0, x=-3 \Rightarrow C$ and $D$. They may set up 4 simultaneous equations and solve to find two of the constants. FYI the equations are $A=3, 3A+B=8, 3B+C+D=-3, 3C=-6$. For division it will be arriving at a linear quotient of the form $3x\pm...$
A1: Two correct constants e.g. $C=-2$ and $D=2$. Allow $3x-1$ as the quotient via the alt method. Condone this just written down, i.e. $A=3, B=-1$
ddM1: Correct method to find all four constants (e.g. by comparing coefficients). Attempts a full method to find all four constants. In the main method this may be achieved by substituting both $x=0, x=-3$ followed by comparing coefficients of $x^3$ and $x^2$ for instance. Other methods can involve substituting other values of $x$. In the alternative method it is for dividing and then setting $\frac{remainder}{x(x+3)} \equiv \frac{C}{x}+\frac{D}{x+3}$ before finding values of $C$ and $D$
A1: $A=3, B=-1, C=-2, D=2$. Allow for these to be embedded within the identity
ALT: (via division) M1: Attempts to divide $3x^3+8x^2-3x-6$ by $x^2+3x$ forming a linear quotient; dM1: Correct method for two constants implied by quotient of $3x+...$; A1: Correct quotient $3x-1$; ddM1: Correct method to find all four constants (e.g. uses PF on $\frac{rem}{x(x+3)}$); A1: $A=3, B=-1, C=-2, D=2$

parts.label: b
parts.text:
A curve has equation
$y = \mathrm{g}(x)$    $x > 0$
Using the answer to part (a),
(b) find $\mathrm{g}'(x)$.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Attempts to differentiate and achieves $\frac{C}{x}+\frac{D}{x+3} \to \frac{...}{x^2}+\frac{...}{(x+3)^2}$
A1ft: Differentiates $Ax+B+\frac{C}{x}+\frac{D}{x+3}$ to $A-\frac{C}{x^2}-\frac{D}{(x+3)^2}$ following through on their constants. Candidates should simplify their coefficients. You may award as above with constants $A, C$ and $D$ instead of the numerical values.
$\mathrm{g}'(x)=3+\dfrac{2}{x^2}-\dfrac{2}{(x+3)^2}$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- $\mathrm{g}(x)=3x-1-\frac{2}{x}+\frac{2}{x+3}$

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Hence, explain why  $\mathrm{g}'(x) > 3$  for all values of $x$ in the domain of g.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: B1: This requires a correct part (a) and a correct (b). Look for a reason and a conclusion. Accept as a minimum $\dfrac{2}{x^2}-\dfrac{2}{(x+3)^2}>0$ so $\mathrm{g}'(x)>3$. Or $\dfrac{2}{x^2}>\dfrac{2}{(x+3)^2}$ so $\mathrm{g}'(x)>3$. Also $3+\dfrac{2}{x^2}-\dfrac{2}{(x+3)^2}=3+\dfrac{2(6x+9)}{x^2(x+3)^2}$ and explains that this is $3+(+ve)>3$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find, in ascending powers of $x$, the first four non-zero terms of the binomial expansion of $\mathrm{f}(x)$. Give each coefficient in simplest form.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: Correct first two terms which does not need to be simplified, so $1+\frac{1}{2}\times -4x^2$ is fine.
M1: Correct attempt at the binomial expansion for term 3 or term 4. Look for $\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}\times-\frac{1}{2}\times(\pm 4x^2)^2}{2}$ or $\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}\times-\frac{1}{2}\times-\frac{3}{2}\times(\pm 4x^2)^3}{3!}$ but condone a failure to square or cube the 4 (i.e. missing brackets). Also award this mark for candidates who mistakenly attempt the binomial expansion of $\sqrt{1-4x}$ to produce either $\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}\times-\frac{1}{2}}{2}(\pm 4x)^2$ or $\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}\times-\frac{1}{2}\times-\frac{3}{2}}{3!}(\pm 4x)^3$. Or $\sqrt{1-x^2}$ to produce either $\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}\times-\frac{1}{2}}{2}(\pm x^2)^2$ or $\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}\times-\frac{1}{2}\times-\frac{3}{2}}{3!}(\pm x^2)^3$
A1: Two correct and simplified terms of $-2x^2, -2x^4, -4x^6$
A1: $1-2x^2-2x^4-4x^6$ or exact simplified equivalent such as $1+(-2)x^2+(-2)x^4+(-4)x^6$. Ignore any additional terms. This may be given separately as a list. $1, -2x^2, -2x^4, -4x^6$
Alt: It is possible to attempt part (a) as $\sqrt{1-4x^2}=(1-2x)^{1/2}\times(1+2x)^{1/2}=\left(1-x-\frac{1}{2}x^2-\frac{1}{2}x^3...\right)\times\left(1+x-\frac{1}{2}x^2+\frac{1}{2}x^3....\right)=1.....$ Score M1 for such an attempt and award the other marks as in the main scheme. As is the main scheme look for a correct attempt at a term 3 or 4 in either bracket followed by an attempt to multiply out
Official notes (completeness pass):
- $\sqrt{1-4x^2}=1-\frac{1}{2}\times 4x^2$ B1; $=1-2x^2-2x^4-4x^6+...$ A1, A1

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) By substituting  $x = \dfrac{1}{4}$  into the binomial expansion of  $\mathrm{f}(x)$, obtain an approximation
for  $\sqrt{3}$
Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Substitutes $x=\frac{1}{4}$ into both sides of (a) and achieves LHS of $\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}}$ or $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. It would be implied by $(\sqrt{3}=)2\times\text{their}\left(1-2\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^2-2\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^4-4\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^6\right)$
A1: 1.7324 Correct answer only here. This is not awrt. Note that the calculator answer is 1.7321
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Substitutes $x=\frac{1}{4}$ into both sides of (a) e.g. $\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}}\approx 1-2\times\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^2-2\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^4-4\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^6$ M1; $\sqrt{3}\approx 1.7324$ cao A1

questions.stem:
Figure 1 shows a sketch of the curve $C$ with parametric equations
$x = 5+2\tan t$    $y = 8\sec^2 t$    $-\dfrac{\pi}{3} \leqslant t \leqslant \dfrac{\pi}{4}$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Use parametric differentiation to find the gradient of $C$ at  $x = 3$
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Attempts to use the rule $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}$. Condone incorrect attempts on $\dfrac{dy}{dt}$ and $\dfrac{dx}{dt}$
A1: A correct expression for $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{16\sec^2 t\tan t}{2\sec^2 t}$ or unsimplified equivalent. Note that there may be many different versions of this including ones that have used double angle formulae. Look carefully
dM1: Dependent upon the previous M. It is for either substituting $\tan t=-1$ into their $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\mathrm{g}(t)$ to find the gradient or substituting $t=-\frac{\pi}{4}$ into their $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\mathrm{g}(t)$ to find the gradient. Condone $t=$ awrt $-0.785$
A1: CSO Gradient $=-8$. This cannot be awarded from differentiation of $y=2(x-5)^2+8$
Gradient $=8\tan t \Rightarrow$ At $x=3, \tan t=-1 \Rightarrow$ Gradient $=-8$

parts.label: b
parts.text:
The curve $C$ has equation  $y = \mathrm{f}(x)$, where f is a quadratic function.
(b) Find  $\mathrm{f}(x)$  in the form  $a(x+b)^2+c$, where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are constants to be found.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Attempts to use $\pm 1\pm\tan^2 t=\pm\sec^2 t$ with $\tan t$ being replaced by an expression in $x$ and $\sec^2 t$ being replaced by an expression in $y$
A1: A correct unsimplified equation $1+\dfrac{(x-5)^2}{4}=\dfrac{y}{8}$ o.e.
A1: $y=2(x-5)^2+8$. $\mathrm{f}(x)=2(x-5)^2+8$ is also fine
NB1: It is possible to use part (a), find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=4(x-5)$, and then integrate using a point such as $(3,16)$ to find "c"
NB2: It is possible to use points to generate $\mathrm{f}(x)$. For the M1 you should expect to see $\mathrm{f}(x)=ax^2+bx+c$, or equivalent, and the use of 3 points to set up 3 simultaneous equations in $a, b$ and $c$ which must be then solved. At least one of three points used must be correct. Examples of possible points that can be used are $(5,8), (3,16), (5-2\sqrt{3},32)$ and $(7,16)$. For the A1 you need to see a correct equation, e.g. $y=2x^2-20x+58$. The final A1 will be $y=2(x-5)^2+8$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- If you see a solution worthy of merit and you cannot see how to award the marks then send to review.

parts.label: c
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: One correct end found, condoning strict inequalities. Look for the lower value of the range to be 8 (or their $c$) or the higher value to be 32
A1: $8 \leqslant \mathrm{f} \leqslant 32$ or equivalent such as $[8,32]$

parts.text:
In this question you must show all stages of your working.
Solutions relying on calculator technology are not acceptable.
Figure 2 shows a sketch of the curve with equation
$y = \dfrac{16\sin 2x}{(3+4\sin x)^2}$    $0 \leqslant x \leqslant \dfrac{\pi}{2}$
The region $R$, shown shaded in Figure 2, is bounded by the curve, the $x$-axis and the line
with equation  $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$
Using the substitution  $u = 3+4\sin x$, show that the area of $R$ can be written in the form
$a + \ln b$, where $a$ and $b$ are rational constants to be found.
(7)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: States or uses $\dfrac{du}{dx}=4\cos x$ o.e. This may be seen within the integrand.
M1: Attempts to write all in terms of $u$. Look for $\int \dfrac{16\sin 2x}{(3+4\sin x)^2}\,dx = \int \dfrac{...\sin x\cos x}{(3+4\sin x)^2}\,dx = \pm\int \dfrac{...(u\pm 3)}{u^2}\,du$. It is common to lose the square on the $u^2$ which would be M0. Only the penultimate mark would then be available.
A1: Correct $\int \dfrac{2(u-3)}{u^2}\,du$ o.e. Allow this to be unsimplified. Condone a missing $du$ this can be implied by further work.
dM1: Integrates $\int \dfrac{...(u\pm 3)}{u^2}\,du$ to $...\ln u \pm \dfrac{...}{u}$ o.e. Condone a missing $du$ this can be implied by further work. Note that $\int \dfrac{...(u\pm 3)}{u^2}\,du \to ...\ln u^2 \pm \dfrac{...}{u}$ is acceptable. You may see attempts using parts: $\int \frac{1}{u^2}\times(2u-6)\,du=-\frac{1}{u}\times(2u-6)-\int -\frac{1}{u}\times 2\,du=-\frac{1}{u}\times(2u-6)+2\ln u$
A1: Correct $2\ln u+\dfrac{6}{u}$. Note that $\ln u^2+\dfrac{6}{u}$ or $-\frac{1}{u}\times(2u-6)+2\ln u$ is also completely correct
M1: Uses limits 5 and 7 within their attempted integral and subtracts. Condone poor attempts at the integration. Alternatively converts their answer in $u$ back to $x$'s using the correct substitution and uses the given limits
A1: $-\dfrac{12}{35}+\ln\dfrac{49}{25}$ or equivalent such as $\ln 1.96-\dfrac{12}{35}$
ISW after a correct answer.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- $\int \frac{16\sin 2x}{(3+4\sin x)^2}dx=\int \frac{32\sin x\cos x}{(3+4\sin x)^2}dx=\int \frac{2(u-3)}{u^2}du$ M1 A1; $=\int \frac{2}{u}-\frac{6}{u^2}du=2\ln u+\frac{6}{u}$ dM1 A1
- Uses limits of 5 and 7 $\Rightarrow 2\ln 7+\frac{6}{7}-2\ln 5-\frac{6}{5}=-\frac{12}{35}+\ln\frac{49}{25}$ M1 A1

questions.stem:
Figure 4 shows a cylindrical tank that contains some water.
The tank has an internal diameter of 8 m and an internal height of 4.2 m.
Water is flowing into the tank at a constant rate of  $(0.6\pi)\,\mathrm{m}^3$  per minute.
There is a tap at point $T$ at the bottom of the tank.
At time $t$ minutes after the tap has been opened,
•   the depth of the water is $h$ metres
•   the water is leaving the tank at a rate of  $(0.15\pi h)\,\mathrm{m}^3$  per minute

parts.label: a
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: States or uses $V=\pi\times 4^2\times h \Rightarrow \dfrac{dV}{dh}=16\pi$ o.e.
B1: States or uses $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=0.6\pi-0.15\pi h$
M1: Attempts to use $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=\dfrac{dV}{dh}\times\dfrac{dh}{dt}$ or equivalent with their $\dfrac{dV}{dh}$ and $\dfrac{dV}{dt}$
A1*: Proceeds to $\dfrac{dh}{dt}=\dfrac{12-3h}{320}$ from a correct statement with no errors seen. The main scheme is acceptable. Note that the answer is given and there may be many "fudged" attempts. If you see $\dfrac{dh}{dt}=\dfrac{1}{16\pi}\times(0.6\pi-0.15\pi h)=\dfrac{12-3h}{320}$ or similar without any explanation or sight of $\dfrac{dV}{dt}$ etc you can award B1 (implied), B1 (implied), M1 (implied), A0* (not fully shown)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Attempts to use $\frac{dV}{dt}=\frac{dV}{dh}\times\frac{dh}{dt} \Rightarrow 0.6\pi-0.15\pi h=16\pi\times\frac{dh}{dt}$ M1

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Given that the depth of the water in the tank is 0.5 m when the tap is opened,
(b) find the time taken for the depth of water in the tank to reach 3.5 m.
(6)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Separates variables and integrates both sides. Look for $\pm a\ln(12-3h)=\pm bt+c$ or equivalent. Note that $\pm a\ln(4-h)=\pm bt+k$ is also correct. There is no need for a constant at this stage. Alternatively $\dfrac{dt}{dh}=\dfrac{320}{12-3h} \Rightarrow t=...\ln(12-3h)+c$. Watch for variations on this such as $t=\ln(4-h)+k$
A1: $-\dfrac{1}{3}\ln(12-3h)=\dfrac{1}{320}t+c$ with or without the $+c$
M1: Uses $t=0, h=0.5$ to find $c$. Condone poor integration and poor attempts to re arrange the equation for this mark.
A1: Correct equation linking $h$ and $t$. This may be implied by an equation with $h$ replaced by 0.5. E.g. $\ln(12-3\times 3.5)=-\dfrac{3}{320}t+\ln 10.5$. Condone $c$ being a decimal (3sf) for this mark. So $\ln(12-3h)=-\dfrac{3}{320}t+2.35$ is fine
dM1: Substitutes $h=3.5$ to find $t$. Dependent upon previous M. Note that $\left[-\frac{1}{3}\ln(12-3h)\right]_{0.5}^{3.5}=\left[\frac{1}{320}t\right]_0^T$ can score 3 marks at once provided they reach a value for $T$
A1: States 207-208 minutes with correct units following correct work. Accept any value between and including these. Condone $\dfrac{320}{3}\ln 7$ minutes
208 minutes cso
Official notes (completeness pass):
- $\frac{dh}{dt}=\frac{12-3h}{320} \Rightarrow \int \frac{dh}{12-3h}=\int \frac{1}{320}dt$; Uses $t=0, h=0.5$: $-\frac{1}{3}\ln\left(\frac{21}{2}\right)=c \Rightarrow -\frac{1}{3}\ln(12-3h)=\frac{1}{320}t-\frac{1}{3}\ln\left(\frac{21}{2}\right)$ M1 A1
- Substitutes $h=3.5$: $-\frac{1}{3}\ln\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)=\frac{1}{320}t-\frac{1}{3}\ln\left(\frac{21}{2}\right) \Rightarrow t=...$ dM1
- This method is similar to $\left[-\frac{1}{3}\ln(12-3h)\right]_{0.5}^{3.5}=\left[\frac{1}{320}t\right]_0^T$ and can score 3 marks on the final line when they subtract

questions.stem:
(a) A student's attempt to answer the question
"Prove by contradiction that if $n^3$ is even, then $n$ is even"
is shown below. Line 5 of the proof is missing.
Assume that there exists a number $n$ such that $n^3$ is even, but $n$ is odd.
If $n$ is odd then  $n = 2p+1$  where  $p \in \mathbb{Z}$
So  $n^3 = (2p+1)^3$
$= 8p^3 + 12p^2 + 6p + 1$
$=$
This contradicts our initial assumption, so if $n^3$ is even, then $n$ is even.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete this proof by filling in line 5.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: B1: See scheme. Requires correct reason/algebra and a statement of the expression being odd. Allow even + even + even + 1 = odd. Allow $2p(4p^2+6p+3)+1=$ odd. Writes $2(4p^3+6p^2+3p)+1$ which is odd

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Hence, prove by contradiction that  $\sqrt[3]{2}$  is irrational.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Sets up the contradiction AND cubes. Condone the omission of the fact that $\dfrac{p}{q}$ is in its simplest form for this mark. Condone as a minimum $\sqrt[3]{2}=\dfrac{p}{q}$ followed by $2=\dfrac{p^3}{q^3}$ o.e.
Assumption: E.g. States that there exists integers $p$ and $q$ such that $\sqrt[3]{2}=\dfrac{p}{q}$ (where $\dfrac{p}{q}$ is in its simplest form) and then cubes to get $2=\dfrac{p^3}{q^3}$
A1: States that $p^3=2q^3$ and concludes both that $p^3$ is even so therefore $p$ is even. Accept other equivalent statements to even such as "multiple of 2". Condone poor explanations so long as they state that both $p^3$ and $p$ are even
M1: Writes $p=2m$ so $(2m)^3=2q^3$ and then attempts to find $q^3=...$
A1: States that $q^3=4m^3$ and concludes that $q^3$ is even so therefore $q$ is even. Accept other equivalent statements to even such as "multiple of 2". Condone poor explanations so long as they state that both $q^3$ and $q$ are even
A1*: Completely correct proof and conclusion with no missing statements. To score this final mark the statements now need to be the correct way around. E.g. $q^3$ is even so therefore $q$ is even. It requires $\dfrac{p}{q}$ to be in simplest form (or equivalent such as no common factor) in the initial assumption. This contradicts our initial statement, as if they both have a factor of 2 it means that $\dfrac{p}{q}$ is not in its simplest form, so $\sqrt[3]{2}$ is irrational
